prompt.context: After returning from a trade show, the CEO of a large grocery distribution center calls you. He enthusiastically describes a new technology which could be used to automate part of his company's process. Knowing that this CEO is a tech-enthusiast who loves innovation for the novelty of it, you ponder the implications.
prompt.question: He asks whether you think this would be a good idea for his business. How would you tackle this problem?

clarifying_info.q: Does the company have a specific financial goal or target in mind?
clarifying_info.a: The company does not have a specific goal in mind. The CEO trusts us and will do whatever we advise.

clarifying_info.q: What is the scale of the operation — how many shipments and to how many customers?
clarifying_info.a: Shipments are made to roughly 50 grocery stores in the immediate area, and the company does 1 million shipments per year.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs to automate?
clarifying_info.a: There is a one-time outlay of $4M, plus recurring overhead, training, and maintenance costs of $1.4M per year (both pieces of info should be requested separately).

exhibits.title: Current Process
exhibits.shows: A process flow diagram of the distribution center's three phases — Receiving, Holding & Picking, and Shipping — with weekly hours for each phase.

data.note: All units are hours per week

exhibits.title: Automated Process
exhibits.shows: The same three-phase distribution process flow showing revised weekly hours after automation is implemented.

framework: Revenues — recognize this is primarily a cost issue; the company is not capacity-constrained and automation will not generate incremental revenue

Costs — Existing: fixed (rent, overhead, salaries) and variable (hourly employees, repairs, inventory holding, shipping); Incremental one-time: automation capex, initial training, severance; Incremental ongoing: servicing, repairs, energy, insurance
Product — assess changes to product quality (none) and ability to distribute new product types (none)
Other — potential future tech synergies; impact on relationships with employees, grocers, and suppliers

questions.prompt: Visualize and describe the distribution center's process flow. What are the three phases of the operation?
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through the end-to-end distribution process: goods arrive (Receiving), are stored and selected for orders (Holding & Picking), then dispatched (Shipping). If the candidate does not spontaneously visualize the process, press them. Confirm the three phases are Receiving, Holding & Picking, and Shipping.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm the potential costs associated with each phase of the distribution process.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify labor (time/wages), equipment (forklifts, conveyors, etc.), insurance, and storage costs (cold and dry) across Receiving, Holding & Picking, and Shipping. Depth and breadth across all three phases is expected.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total number of employees required in each function and the total annual labor cost under the current process.
questions.guidance: Candidate must divide total weekly hours by 40 hrs/employee to find headcount, then multiply by hourly rate and 52 weeks. Interviewer provides wage rates only if asked: Receiving $12/hr, Holding & Picking $17/hr, Shipping $14/hr. Force use of 52 weeks (not 50).

math.setup: Employees = Total weekly hours / 40 hrs per employee. Weekly cost = Total weekly hours x hourly rate. Annual cost = Weekly cost x 52.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the change in headcount and annual labor cost under the automated process, and determine the annual labor savings.
questions.guidance: Repeat the same calculation structure with the new hours. Note Receiving is unchanged; Holding & Picking drops sharply; Shipping increases. Candidate should net out the change.

math.setup: Same formula applied to Exhibit 2 hours, then compare to current figures.
steps: Headcount change: Receiving 0, Holding & Picking -119 (rounded), Shipping +75; net reduction ~44 employees
math.answer: Automated annual cost $10,257,000; annual labor savings $2,015,000; net headcount reduction ~44

questions.prompt: Calculate the break-even period (in years) for the automation investment, incorporating both the one-time capex and the incremental ongoing costs.
questions.guidance: Candidate must net the annual savings against the incremental recurring costs to get annual incremental contribution margin, then divide the one-time outlay by that figure. Strong candidates note that the recurring OH/training/maintenance cost is $1.4M but only $1.2M is used as annual incremental costs in the model — use $1.2M as provided. Ask whether a ~5-year payback is attractive given the prompt context (CEO motivated by novelty, not strategy).

math.setup: Annual incremental CM = Annual labor savings - Annual incremental ongoing costs. Break-even = One-time outlay / Annual incremental CM.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential costs associated with each phase of the distribution process — Receiving, Holding & Picking, and Shipping?

categories.name: Labor
ideas: Hourly wages for pickers, receivers, loaders
Severance for displaced workers if automation reduces headcount

recommendation: Do not automate at this time — the ~5-year payback period is financially marginal and inconsistent with the CEO's stated motivation of pursuing technology for its novelty
The annual incremental contribution margin of only $815,000 against a $4M outlay ties up significant capital with no strategic revenue upside
risks: If the CEO proceeds for novelty reasons alone, capital is locked for ~5 years with limited flexibility
Automation shifts headcount from Holding & Picking to Shipping, creating workforce transition risk and potential morale issues
Technology obsolescence risk — the new system may be superseded before the payback is achieved
Shipping hours nearly double under automation, increasing labor cost in that function and creating execution risk
next_steps: Conduct a full strategic review to determine whether there are revenue-side or capacity-growth scenarios that could improve the ROI
Assess workforce implications and model total severance/transition costs not captured in current analysis
Evaluate whether the technology integrates with future systems (synergy potential) before making a final capital commitment
If the CEO remains interested, consider piloting automation in one phase (e.g., Holding & Picking) to validate cost savings before full rollout
